title: Anchor text analysis and contextual hyperlink indexing
summary: The original PageRank paper reasons that anchor text often describes a page better than the page itself. Google's current link guidance asks for descriptive, concise, relevant anchors, warns against cramming keywords, and says links must be <a> elements with an href to be reliably crawled. Paid and user-generated links should carry rel=sponsored or rel=ugc. No saved source says exact-match anchors outrank descriptive ones.
actions: Replace generic or stuffed anchors with descriptive, concise text.
Check navigation uses <a href>, not click handlers.
Mark paid links sponsored and UGC links ugc.

myths.myth: Exact-match anchor text should be used on every link.
myths.correction: Google asks for descriptive, concise anchors and says to resist cramming keywords.

items.prompt: Brin and Page say anchors often provide more accurate what of web pages than the pages themselves? One word.
items.explanation: The paper says anchors often provide more accurate descriptions of web pages than the pages themselves. This is the paper's reasoning, not a statement about Google's current systems.

items.prompt: Which description of good anchor text does Google give in its link best practices?
options: A. Packed with every related keyword you can fit
B. Identical on every single link across the site
C. Descriptive, reasonably concise and relevant to the linked page
D. Only a short generic label such as 'click here'
items.explanation: Correct: Google says good anchor text is descriptive, reasonably concise, and relevant to the page that it's on. Wrong: 'Packed with every related keyword you can fit' - Google says to resist the urge to cram in every related keyword. 'Identical on every single link across the site' - the page asks for relevance to the linked page, not uniform text. 'Only a short generic label such as 'click here'' - a bare label is not descriptive.

items.prompt: True or false: Google says it can only crawl a link if it is an <a> HTML element.
items.explanation: The link best practices page says Google can only crawl your link if it's an <a> element, and elsewhere says it cannot reliably extract URLs from <a> elements without an href.

items.prompt: According to the 1998 paper, what is the first reason it gives for using anchor text?
options: A. Anchors often describe pages better than pages do
B. Anchors are never keyword stuffed by site owners
C. Anchors always pass the target page's full PageRank along
D. Anchors remove the need for any page title at all
items.explanation: Correct: the paper says anchors often provide more accurate descriptions of web pages than the pages themselves. This is the paper's design reasoning only. Wrong: 'Anchors are never keyword stuffed by site owners' - no such claim appears in the quote. 'Anchors always pass the target page's full PageRank along' - the quote is about description, not PageRank transfer. 'Anchors remove the need for any page title at all' - the paper does not say titles become unnecessary.

items.prompt: True or false: Google's link guidance recommends fitting every keyword related to the page into the anchor text.
items.explanation: The page says to resist the urge to cram every related keyword into anchor text and to keep it descriptive and concise.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the saved sources?
options: A. Google recommends sponsored for paid placements
B. Google recommends ugc for comment and forum links
C. Links with these rel values will generally not be followed
D. Google confirmed exact-match anchors rank higher
items.explanation: Correct: no saved Google source says exact-match anchors outrank descriptive anchors; the guidance asks for descriptive, concise, relevant text. Wrong: 'Google recommends sponsored for paid placements' - supported by the qualify-links page. 'Google recommends ugc for comment and forum links' - supported by the same page. 'Links with these rel values will generally not be followed' - supported: the page says so, while pages may still be found by other means.

items.prompt: Hypothetical: you link to a page about an online store's returns process. Which anchor best follows Google's guidance?
options: A. click here
B. returns policy for online orders
C. returns returns policy returns online store refund
D. here
items.explanation: Correct: it is descriptive, reasonably concise and relevant to the target page. Wrong: 'click here' - not descriptive. 'returns returns policy returns online store refund' - crams keywords, which Google says to resist. 'here' - not descriptive.

items.prompt: An audit note says: 'The mega-menu items are <a onclick="goto(...)"> with no href; Google will follow them as normal links.' What is wrong?
options: A. Menu links must always carry rel=nofollow to be valid
B. Anchors in menus cannot hold any visible text
C. Google can't reliably extract URLs without href
D. Google ignores every link that sits inside a menu
items.explanation: Correct: Google lists <a> elements without an href as links it cannot reliably extract URLs from; use <a href> links. Wrong: 'Menu links must always carry rel=nofollow to be valid' - no saved source says menus need nofollow. 'Anchors in menus cannot hold any visible text' - anchors can hold text; the problem is the missing href. 'Google ignores every link that sits inside a menu' - the page does not say menu links are ignored.

items.prompt: Hypothetical JS storefront 'GearBox'. Evidence: (1) category links are buttons with click handlers, not <a href>; (2) only the home page appears in the index; (3) Google's JavaScript docs describe crawl, render and index phases. Best fix?
options: A. Add more keywords to the page title and headings
B. Mark the buttons as rel=sponsored to speed discovery
C. Raise the number of sitemap files submitted
D. Use real <a href> links to the category paths, with clear descriptive anchors
items.explanation: Correct: Google says it can only crawl <a> HTML elements, and it cannot reliably extract URLs from <a> elements without an href. Wrong: 'Add more keywords to the page title and headings' - titles do not create links. 'Mark the buttons as rel=sponsored to speed discovery' - sponsored is for paid links and would not make them crawlable. 'Raise the number of sitemap files submitted' - extra sitemaps do not give the buttons href values.

items.prompt: Hypothetical blog 'TrailNotes'. Evidence: (1) an agency set every internal link to a product page to the same long phrase listing five related keywords; (2) Google's link guidance says to resist cramming every related keyword into anchors; (3) Google's spam policy defines keyword stuffing as filling a page with keywords or numbers to manipulate rankings, and lists repeating words so often it sounds unnatural as an example. Best action?
options: A. Rewrite as descriptive, concise anchors
B. Keep them; repetition builds authority over time and across the site
C. Add rel=ugc to each internal link on the page
D. Delete all internal links to the page
items.explanation: Correct: descriptive, concise, relevant anchors match Google's guidance and avoid cramming keywords. Whether this alone changes rankings is unconfirmed. Wrong: 'Keep them; repetition builds authority over time and across the site' - Google's guidance points the other way. 'Add rel=ugc to each internal link on the page' - ugc is for user-generated content and does not fix the text. 'Delete all internal links to the page' - Google says every page you care about should be linked from another page.
